newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan adopts new measures to deal with disasters.
newsitem.headline: Japan adopts new measures to deal with disasters.

text.p: Japan on Tuesday announced measures to deal with disasters following a string of natural and man-made calamities in the past two years.
The measures focus on the handling and prevention of "large-scale modern artificial disasters" including nuclear accidents, oil spills and aviation mishaps.
Previous government disaster guidelines had targeted only natural disasters, especially large earthquakes.

"The development in recent years of an advanced transport system, the increased use of nuclear power plants...call for measures to prevent disasters," said a report released by a panel headed by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
The 375-page anti-disaster prevention guidelines say the prime minister should form and take command of any emergency task force without first getting cabinet approval.
It also calls for the country's military to swiftly engage in rescue operations and collect information for the prime minister during disasters.
The measures followed public criticism of the handling of the 1995 Kobe earthquake relief effort, along with Japan's worst oil spill and a nuclear accident, both this year.

"In the event of an accident, the government must probe the cause and prevent the repeat of similar disasters by implementing anti-disaster measures," the report said, referring specifically to nuclear mishaps.
In the event of an atomic accident, the government plans to set up an emergency rescue unit to monitor and prevent radiation leakages, a government official said.

When a fire broke out at a processing plant near Tokyo in March, scores of workers were exposed to low level radiation. Officials at the state-run nuclear company did not promptly report the accident to Prime Minister Hashimoto.
The accident fuelled demands for a wholesale review or overhaul of the country's nuclear safety standards and nuclear programme.
The report also called for cooperation by central and local governments to provide accurate information on ocean routes to help ensure safe shipping.
It also urged shipping companies to have equipment available to clean up oil spills.
In January, a Russian-owned tanker carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of fuel oil broke in half in stormy seas in the Sea of Japan causing Japan's worst oil spill disaster.
Apart from the death of four people including the captain of the tanker, the spill badly polluted a wide stretch of rich fishing grounds and many popular tourist beaches.
